analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act and replaces it with high-risk pools, association plans, and insurance sales across state lines.
analysis.headline: The full repeal bill was referred to eight House committees on the day it was introduced, never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal the Affordable Care Act and the 2010 health care reconciliation law as if they had never passed, erasing the coverage expansions, subsidies, insurance rules, and tax increases in one stroke. In their place it would fund state high-risk pools for people with preexisting conditions, pay states bonuses for cutting premiums and uninsured rates, let small businesses band together in association health plans, allow insurance to be sold across state lines, cap medical-malpractice damages, and expand health savings accounts. It keeps a few ACA-style consumer protections, such as a ban on lifetime spending caps and coverage for young adults through age 25, but strips the individual market's guaranteed-issue and premium-rating rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Higher-income households who paid the Affordable Care Act's tax increases; healthier insurance buyers whose premiums would fall once insurers could price for health status again; small businesses and trade associations that could form cheaper association health plans; medical device makers and other industries whose excise taxes would disappear; and people with preexisting conditions who could reach a well-funded state high-risk pool.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, device makers, healthier insurance buyers

how_it_helps.text: It appropriates $25 billion over ten years for state high-risk pools and reinsurance programs, with pool premiums capped at 150% of standard market rates, no waiting lists, and coverage for people stuck in the two-year Medicare disability waiting period.
It appropriates roughly $48 billion in bonus payments to states that reduce premiums in the individual and small-group markets or lower the share of uninsured residents.
It bans annual and lifetime aggregate spending caps in health insurance plans, with an exception for plans that would face a significant premium increase.
It requires independent external review before an insurer can cancel an individual policy, with coverage remaining in effect while the review proceeds.
It keeps dependent coverage through age 25, allows health savings account funds to pay premiums for high-deductible plans, and adds a saver's credit for HSA contributions.
It repeals the Affordable Care Act and its tax increases in their entirety, including the provisions of the 2010 reconciliation law.

analysis.who_pays: People with preexisting conditions would pay up to 150% of standard premiums in high-risk pools or fall outside guaranteed-issue protections; lower-income people who would have gained Medicaid or subsidies would lose them; seniors would again pay the full cost of drugs in the Medicare coverage gap; taxpayers would fund the roughly $75 billion in pool and state-bonus appropriations; and injured patients would face capped malpractice awards.
analysis.who_pays_short: Sicker patients, the uninsured, seniors, taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Repealing the Affordable Care Act would have ended the premium subsidies, the Medicaid expansion, and the guaranteed-availability rules in the individual market, replacing them only with state high-risk pools that the bill would fund at $25 billion over a decade.
High-risk pool premiums could legally run to 150% of the average standard market rate, so people with serious conditions would pay far more than healthy buyers of the same age.
Interstate sales would apply the law of a plan's designated primary state nationwide, letting insurers base themselves in whichever state had the weakest consumer rules and sell into every other one.
Repealing the 2010 laws would have reopened the Medicare prescription-drug coverage gap, restoring higher out-of-pocket drug costs for seniors.
The bill caps noneconomic and punitive damages in health-care liability suits and sets a statute of limitations, limiting what injured patients can recover.
Group plans could vary premiums and cost-sharing by up to 50% based on whether a worker participates in a wellness program, imposing heavier charges on workers who decline.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill kept a handful of genuinely popular protections, including the ban on lifetime spending caps, rescission review, and young-adult coverage, and its high-risk pool funding was more generous than some earlier proposals. But those pieces sat on top of a full repeal whose largest financial effects ran the other way: the tax increases that paid for the coverage expansion would be gone, the insurance-market rules protecting sicker buyers would be weakened, and the interstate-sales and tort provisions shifted risk onto patients and state regulators. Weighed honestly, the repeal far outweighed the replacement in scale and would have left people with costly conditions paying more for less certain coverage.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to eight House committees on January 24, 2011, was later sent to two subcommittees, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Representative Wally Herger of California introduced the bill on January 24, 2011, joined by a dozen Republican colleagues as original cosponsors.

The same day, the Speaker referred it to eight committees: Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Education and the Workforce, Judiciary, House Administration, Natural Resources, Appropriations, and Rules.
In February 2011 portions were referred to the Health Subcommittee and the Subcommittee on Indian and Alaska Native Affairs; no committee ever reported the bill.
The bill drew 17 cosponsors, all of them Republicans.
No further action appears in the record through January 3, 2013, when the 112th Congress ended and the bill expired.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Affordable Care Act stayed on the books, so its coverage expansions, insurance rules, and taxes continued to operate; no industry received the deregulation the bill offered, and the state bonus and high-risk pool money was never spent.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Those who kept Affordable Care Act protections

for.name: Rep. Wally Herger
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the full repeal-and-replace bill on January 24, 2011.

for.name: 17 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 17 were Republicans, including the 12 members who joined at introduction.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and never held a hearing or markup, nor reported the bill to the floor.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for floor consideration, leaving it parked across eight committees after a separate standalone repeal measure passed the House in January 2011.

against.name: Senate Democratic majority
against.what_they_did: Controlled the Senate and took no action on any companion full-repeal measure, ensuring the bill could not have become law even if the House had passed it.

against.name: President Barack Obama
against.what_they_did: Opposed repeal of his signature health law; any repeal bill reaching his desk would have been vetoed.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 17 cosponsors were Republicans and no Democrat sponsored the bill; no recorded vote was ever taken, so the fight never got past the all-Republican sponsorship stage.

industries.note: Repeal would take away the mandate and subsidies that steered millions of subsidized customers to insurers, but it would also strip ACA insurance rules and let plans sell nationwide under the rules of a self-chosen, lightly regulated primary state. The bill's deregulatory provisions benefit insurers at the expense of consumer protections, while repeal costs them their guaranteed customer base.

Repeal would erase the Affordable Care Act's tax increases, including the higher Medicare payroll and investment-income taxes that financed coverage expansions. The revenue loss is a direct gain to high earners and comes out of the public's coverage financing.
Repeal would eliminate the ACA's excise tax on medical devices. Device makers gain directly, with at most a small indirect benefit to patients through device prices.

Repealing the 2010 laws would reopen the Medicare coverage gap, so seniors would again pay full price for prescriptions, a direct gain to drug makers at seniors' expense; the bill's biosimilar approval pathway is a modest offset.

Association health plans would let business associations pool members for cheaper coverage, though pooled plans that skirt state benefit rules can leave enrollees with thinner benefits if claims run high.
Federal caps on noneconomic and punitive damages would shrink recoveries for injured patients and the fees that flow from them; patients and the plaintiffs' bar lose together under this provision.
